current_episode.title: Stuart Foster and Brian Holland, NatWest Group

guest.titre: Director, Customer Vulnerability, Retail Controls and Remediation
guest.bio_context: Brian Holland has been with NatWest for 14 years and leads the bank's approach to vulnerable customers, including consumer duty, retail bank risk and control environment, and remediation activities. Stuart Foster has been with NatWest for 24 years and is responsible for delivering all products and services to institutional clients ranging from banks to funds to insurance companies. Both co-authored the joint foreword to Responsible Finance's 2023 impact report, published in May 2024 at an event hosted by NatWest.

context.real_quote: CDFIs provide a terrific part of the overall ecosystem of financial services — for those who are not able to borrow from the mainstream banks, CDFIs do a brilliant job filling that gap.
key_stats: NatWest has worked with the UK community finance sector for over 30 years, active since the mid-1990s
NatWest provided over £1 million in funding and technical assistance to Responsible Finance (then Community Development Finance Association) between 2008 and 2012
NatWest Social and Community Capital (S&CC) was set up in 1999 — the only bank-owned CDFI vehicle of its kind in the UK

NatWest was part of the Merlin Agreement in 2009, one of four banks providing £50 million of investment to create Big Society Capital (now Better Society Capital); Stuart Foster served on the Better Society Capital board for 6.5 years
NatWest's total cost of living support package was approximately £10 million; £900,000 was allocated to Responsible Finance for the Hardship Grant Programme
NatWest waived around £70 million in fees and interest charges to customers directed to its financial health and support area during the cost of living crisis
The Hardship Grant Programme: £416,000 dispersed by 6 CDFIs, average grant of £102, approximately 4,000 families helped; 62% of recipients were women, 66% aged 25–44
Know My Credit Score has been accessed 83 million times over 12 months by NatWest's 17 million customers

Brian is joined by NatWest Group's Stuart Foster, Managing Director of Financial Institutions. And today's podcast covers topics including NatWest Group's support for and work with Community Development Finance Institution. We learn more about NatWest's work with CDFIs over three decades, about the Hardship Grant Programme in 2023, which also came with capacity building support for CDFIs. Brian and Stuart also discuss referring people, businesses and social enterprises to CDFIs, investment into the CDFI sector and what policy tools might make this easier. Plus the significance of a record year of lending for CDFIs and investment into the sector. Brian, Stuart, thanks ever so much for joining us on the Responsible Finance Podcast today. Welcome both of you. Hello, how are we? Good morning. Good morning indeed. Thank you both for joining. So first of all, I'm going to ask each of you how long you've been with NatWest and what your role involves. Can we kick off with you, Brian? Yes, certainly. I've been with NatWest now 14 years. I head up across the bank, our approach to our vulnerable customers. And what that means in practical terms is I also lead on consumer duty, but also lead within the retail bank on our risk and control environment, as well as our remediation activities when we look to get things right for customers. And what about you, Stuart, your involvement with the bank? How long has that been? So I've been with the bank for 24 years now, which is perhaps giving away my age. And I look after financial institutions across NatWest, which really means I'm responsible for delivering all the products and services that NatWest can offer to a set of institutional clients ranging from banks to funds to insurance companies and ensuring we do that in the best possible way. Super. Well, we're releasing this episode as Responsible Finance publishes its 2023 impact report published in May 2024 at an event hosted by NatWest. And in your joint forward to the report, you've mentioned that NatWest has worked with the UK community finance sector for 30 years. Some of our listeners won't actually be aware of this long and rich history of working with the sector. Can you tell us a little bit more about NatWest's work with CDFIs over those decades, Stuart? Yeah, very happy to. And actually, NatWest has been visible and active in the community finance sector since the mid 1990s. In the last couple of decades, we've been one of the biggest contributors to the UK community finance sector, providing finance and expertise to both the sector body and individual CDFIs. We were actually a founding funder and partner of the community finance membership body Responsible Finance and its previous name, Community Development Finance Association, and have provided over a million pounds in funding and technical assistance programmes between 2008 and 2012 to help the sector. We actually have our own CDFI, NatWest Social and Community Capital, our acronym to S&CC, which we set up in 1999, and that continues to operate today. In fact, we're the only bank to have a vehicle like S&CC, which has allowed us to have very close involvement with the sector over the course of many years. And as such, we've had very good relations with a number of the organisations, including Midlands Community Finance and Salad Money, and obviously Responsible Finance. And then finally, and a bit more personally, we were part of the Merlin Agreement in 2009, where we were one of four banks that provided £50 million of investment to create big society capital, now called Better Society Capital. pending_qa.q: What is NatWest's 'Know My Credit Score' initiative and how does it relate to the CDFI ecosystem?
pending_qa.r: Know My Credit Score is a NatWest service that gives customers free access to their credit score and tips on how to improve it; it has been accessed 83 million times over 12 months by NatWest's 17 million customers. NatWest recently extended free access to anyone with its mobile app, even without a financial product. The initiative is intended to help individuals build their credit records over time so they can eventually qualify for mainstream lending, with CDFIs serving as the responsible credit provider in the interim period.

pending_qa.q: What policy tools and funding mechanisms could help scale investment into the CDFI sector according to NatWest?
pending_qa.r: Stuart Foster highlighted the Dormant Assets Fund as a potential source of catalytic capital that could unlock private capital from mainstream lenders and other sources, though he acknowledged it is not a silver bullet on its own. First loss funding structures and other financial mechanisms that de-risk investment were identified as fundamental to the sector's growth over the next few years. NatWest also emphasised the importance of collaboration with partners including Fair by Design, Responsible Finance, CDFIs themselves, and the FCA to increase the absolute volume of capital flowing into the sector.

pending_qa.q: Why is 2023 being described as a record-breaking year for CDFI lending and why does NatWest consider this significant?
pending_qa.r: The cost of living crisis drove greater volumes of individuals and businesses to CDFIs, contributing to a record year of lending across the sector. NatWest views this as significant because it demonstrates CDFIs' essential role in a diverse finance ecosystem that serves customers who cannot meet mainstream bank affordability and credit rating requirements. The record lending underscores the need for continued investment and scaling of CDFIs so they can sustainably fill the gap between mainstream banks and illegal high-interest lenders.

pending_qa.q: Is NatWest open to providing direct investment or lending to CDFIs as part of its ongoing support for the sector?
pending_qa.r: Brian Holland confirmed unequivocally that NatWest is open for business and committed to working with CDFIs, having done so for over 30 years through various approaches. The bank's goal is to help CDFIs scale safely while ensuring they have the right liquidity to support their customers sustainably and grow as businesses. While commercial sensitivities prevent disclosure of specifics, NatWest stated it will continue to work with Responsible Finance and sector members to find ways to remain involved.
